title: What is forwarding vs redistributing data pattern in Flink — forwarding is 1:1 (data stays in same partition, preserves order, e.g. source→map) vs redistributing (data shuffled across subtasks, e.g. after keyBy()) — and how does this affect parallelism and performance?
shortTitle: Forwarding vs redistributing data in Flink

s1_definition.profdef: In Flink, the way data moves between two connected operators is either a forwarding pattern or a redistributing pattern. Forwarding is a one-to-one connection where each subtask of the upstream operator sends its records directly to exactly one corresponding subtask of the downstream operator, keeping records in the same partition, preserving their order, and requiring no network shuffle. Redistributing is a many-to-many connection where records are repartitioned across all downstream subtasks according to a rule such as hashing on a key, which involves a network shuffle, may change ordering across the stream, and is what `keyBy`, `rebalance`, `broadcast`, and `rescale` produce.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has three clerks reading transaction slips and three accountants recording them. Forwarding is like clerk one always handing to accountant one, clerk two to accountant two, and clerk three to accountant three, so each slip stays on its own conveyor belt, in order, with no shuffling between belts. Redistributing is like requiring that all slips for the same account must go to the same accountant regardless of which clerk read them, so the slips get sorted and shuffled across belts to the right accountant, which costs time and mixing but guarantees that all of Rajesh's slips land together.
s1_definition.oneliner: Forwarding keeps records on the same lane in order with no shuffle, while redistributing shuffles records across lanes by a rule like key hashing at a network cost.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Flink, the way data moves between two connected operators is either a forwarding pattern or a redistributing pattern. Forwarding is a one-to-one connection where each subtask of the upstream operator sends its records directly to exactly one corresponding subtask of the downstream operator, keeping records in the same partition, preserving their order, and requiring no network shuffle. Redistributing is a many-to-many connection where records are repartitioned across all downstream subtasks according to a rule such as hashing on a key, which involves a network shuffle, may change ordering across the stream, and is what `keyBy`, `rebalance`, `broadcast`, and `rescale` produce.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has three clerks reading transaction slips and three accountants recording them. Forwarding is like clerk one always handing to accountant one, clerk two to accountant two, and clerk three to accountant three, so each slip stays on its own conveyor belt, in order, with no shuffling between belts. Redistributing is like requiring that all slips for the same account must go to the same accountant regardless of which clerk read them, so the slips get sorted and shuffled across belts to the right accountant, which costs time and mixing but guarantees that all of Rajesh's slips land together.

**One line to remember:** Forwarding keeps records on the same lane in order with no shuffle, while redistributing shuffles records across lanes by a rule like key hashing at a network cost.

sections.s2_technical:
When you chain operators, Flink connects them with one of two edge types. A forwarding edge appears when consecutive operators have the same parallelism and you have not introduced any repartitioning operation, for example `source.map(...).filter(...)`. Each parallel instance of the source feeds exactly one parallel instance of the map and filter, so records never cross the network between subtasks; they stay inside the same slot, order is preserved within that partition, and Flink can even fuse these operators together into a single task chain that runs in one thread, which is extremely efficient because there is no serialization or network hop.

A redistributing edge appears whenever the data must be repartitioned. The most common cause is `keyBy`, which hashes each record's key and routes it to the downstream subtask responsible for that key's hash bucket, guaranteeing that all records with the same key reach the same subtask so keyed state and keyed aggregations work correctly. Other redistributing operations are `rebalance`, which round-robins records to spread load evenly, `rescale`, which redistributes to a local subset for efficiency, `broadcast`, which sends every record to every downstream subtask, and a custom `partitionCustom`. Redistribution requires serializing each record, sending it over the network to the target subtask, and deserializing it, which is the single most expensive thing a streaming job does, and it generally breaks the strict global ordering because records from many sources interleave at the receiver.

The performance implications are significant. Forwarding edges let Flink build operator chains that avoid network and serialization entirely, so you want to keep as much of your pipeline forwarding as possible. Every redistribution is a shuffle boundary that costs CPU for serialization, network bandwidth, and potential backpressure if a downstream subtask is slow. However, redistribution is often unavoidable and correct: you must `keyBy` before a keyed aggregation or keyed state, and you may need `rebalance` to fix data skew where one forwarding partition carries far more load than others. The senior nuance is to minimize the number of shuffles, place filtering and projection before a `keyBy` so you shuffle less data, be aware that a `keyBy` with a skewed key distribution can overload one subtask and cripple parallelism, and remember that a forwarding chain is only possible when parallelism matches, so changing parallelism between operators forces a redistribution. Choosing where your shuffle boundaries fall is one of the main levers for Flink job performance.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India streams raw transaction records and first wants to clean them, dropping internal test transactions and extracting only the fields it needs. This cleaning is independent per record and does not care which account a record belongs to, so it should stay on the same lane as the source with no shuffle, preserving order and cost. This is exactly the forwarding pattern: source to filter to map all run one-to-one and can be chained into a single efficient task.

Problem 2 — After cleaning, the bank wants a per-account running total, which requires that every transaction for a given account reaches the same computing instance so its state accumulates correctly. Transactions for one account can originate from many source lanes, so they must be shuffled so that, for example, all of Rajesh's transactions land on the same subtask. This is exactly the redistributing pattern caused by keyBy, which hashes the account id and routes accordingly, at the cost of a network shuffle.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that simulates parallel subtasks and shows both patterns. We define a `RawTxn` and a `CleanTxn`. A `ForwardingStage` simulates three parallel lanes each running filter-then-map one-to-one, keeping each record on its own lane and preserving order. A `RedistributingStage` simulates a keyBy by hashing the account id to decide which of three downstream subtasks receives each cleaned record, so all records for one account converge on one subtask where a per-account total accumulates. A `PartitioningDemo` main class feeds raw transactions spread across the three input lanes, shows the forwarding stage keeping them on their lanes, shows the redistributing stage shuffling them by account hash, and prints the per-account totals plus how many cross-lane shuffles happened.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three input lanes carrying Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) transactions, with one internal test transaction, processed by a forwarding stage then a redistributing keyBy stage with three downstream subtasks.

Step 1: Lane zero runs the forwarding stage. It filters out the internal test transaction and maps the remaining two into clean transactions, keeping them on lane zero in order. No record crosses to another lane; this is a pure forwarding, chainable stage.

Step 2: Lanes one and two likewise run the forwarding stage independently, each producing its clean transactions on its own lane. At this point three lanes hold cleaned transactions, and no shuffle has occurred, so this entire portion could be fused into efficient operator chains.

Step 3: The redistributing stage begins. For each clean transaction, the account id is hashed modulo three to pick the target subtask. All Rajesh transactions hash to the same subtask and all Priya transactions hash to the same subtask, regardless of which lane they came from. This guarantees keyed correctness.

Step 4: As records are routed, any record whose target subtask differs from its source lane counts as a cross-lane shuffle, meaning it was serialized and sent over the network. The demo counts these to make the shuffle cost visible, which in a real cluster is the dominant expense.

Step 5: Each subtask accumulates a per-account total as records arrive. Because the keyBy guaranteed all of one account's records converge on one subtask, the totals are correct: Rajesh's total sums 100, 300, and 600 plus his lane-zero 100 for the full amount, and Priya's total sums her transactions across all lanes.

Step 6: The demo prints the final per-account totals and the number of cross-lane shuffles, showing both that the forwarding stage was shuffle-free and that the redistributing stage paid a shuffle cost to achieve keyed correctness.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In Flink, every connection between two operators is either a forwarding edge or a redistributing edge, and knowing the difference is central to writing fast jobs. A forwarding edge is a one-to-one connection: when two consecutive operators have the same parallelism and you have not introduced any repartitioning, each upstream subtask feeds exactly one downstream subtask, so records stay in the same partition, their order is preserved, and nothing crosses the network. Because of this, Flink can fuse forwarding operators into a single task chain that runs in one thread with no serialization and no network hop, which is the most efficient thing a streaming job can do. A good example is a source followed by a filter followed by a map, which all run one-to-one and chain together.

A redistributing edge appears whenever records must be repartitioned. The classic cause is keyBy, which hashes each record's key and routes it to the downstream subtask responsible for that key, guaranteeing that all records with the same key converge on one subtask so keyed state and keyed aggregations are correct. Other redistributing operations are rebalance for round-robin load spreading, rescale for local redistribution, broadcast which sends every record to every subtask, and custom partitioning. Redistribution is expensive because each record is serialized, sent over the network, and deserialized, and it generally breaks strict global ordering because records interleave at the receiver. So the performance rule is to minimize the number of shuffles, keep as much of the pipeline forwarding as possible, and push filtering and projection before a keyBy so you shuffle less data. You also have to watch for key skew, because a keyBy on a lopsided key can dump most records onto one subtask and destroy your effective parallelism.

At the National Bank of India this showed up clearly in our transaction pipeline. The cleaning part, where we dropped internal test transactions and projected only the fields we needed, was per-record and account-agnostic, so it stayed as a forwarding chain fused with the source, costing nothing in network. Then we needed a per-account running total, which required that every transaction for an account reach the same instance, so we did a keyBy on the account id, which is a redistributing shuffle that routes by hash. I deliberately placed the filtering and projection before the keyBy so the shuffle carried less data, and I monitored per-subtask load because a few very high-volume corporate accounts could skew the hash and overload one subtask, in which case we would consider salting the key. Being able to explain where the shuffle boundaries fall, why forwarding chains are free while redistribution is the dominant cost, and how key skew can silently cripple parallelism is exactly what demonstrates real Flink performance expertise.
